who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Abstract: Hul’q’umi’num’ storytellers often use rhetorical lengthening, characterized by a high, steady pitch, to direct attention to certain words or to move the listeners’ attention along in the story. In this study, based on 91 tokens of rhetorical lengthening from six stories told by Mrs. Jimmy Joe, we highlight the prosodic features of rhetorical lengthening and also discuss the meanings it conveys and its use in narrative structure.

form: Coast Salish culture is centered on performance and storytelling, and Hul’q’umi’num’ storytellers are virtuosos in holding the attention of the audience with various narrative devices. This paper studies rhetorical lengthening — the stretching out of the pronunciation of a word to add meaning or convey a narrative effect and to enliven the performance.1 Here is a typical example of rhetorical lengthening on the verb ʔiməš ‘walk’, indicated by repeating the vowel (V.V.V) in the data and labelling it as RL in the gloss.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Halkomelem is one of twenty-three Salish languages currently or historically spoken in what is now known as British Columbia, Idaho, Montana, Oregon, and Washington. Hul’q’umi’num’, the Vancouver Island dialect of Halkomelem (ISO 639-3: hur), is the focus of this study. The territory of the Hul’q’umi’num’ people extends along the Salish Sea from Nanoose to Malahat on Vancouver Island and on neighboring islands in British Columbia, Canada. Today around thirty fluent first-language speakers remain, mostly over the age of seventy, and thus Hul’q’umi’num’ is considered an endangered language. However, amongst the population of over six thousand Hul’q’umi’num’, there are many people who desire to learn the language or to improve their fluency. This research on rhetorical lengthening is part of a project that seeks to inform language instructors and students about storytelling skills, to help unlock their Hul’q’umi’num’ fluency. Our sound archive of legacy stories gives us an opportunity to enjoy story performances and study them for their linguistic features. This study draws on recordings by speaker Mrs. Jimmy Joe (née Ellen Rice), Tixulwut. Mrs. Joe, who was from Penelakut and married and lived at Snuneymuxw First Nation for her adult life, was particularly well-known for her storytelling skills, and many elders have fond memories of hearing her speak in the language.

form: These six stories from Mrs. Joe were examined:

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: • Deserted Boy (DB) — 08:05 minutes, 66 lines • The Sea Hunters and the Dwarves (SHD) — 12:00 minutes, 90 lines • Snake Island (SI) — 3:40 minutes, 47 lines • Pitchy Log Man (Pitch) — 11:32 minutes, 122 lines • Ghost Lover (GL) — 7:00 minutes, 56 lines • The Origin of Sockeye (Sockeye) — 04:23 minutes, 32 lines Our corpus is thus 47:42 minutes and 366 lines. Mrs. Joe uses rhetorical lengthening 91 times in this corpus, so on an average of once every half minute or four lines. Nevertheless, we are left with the impression that many words that could be lengthened are not, and so we see that she uses rhetorical lengthening for special circumstances, and we try to discern what they are by studying the text and the translation. In ascribing reasons for use of rhetorical lengthening, we are not trying so much to make claims about Mrs. Joe’s conscious manipulation of rhetorical lengthening so much as the net effect on the listener, in an aim to understand the strategies that underly rhetorical lengthening usage.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: We assembled a database that coded phonetics (Section 3), semantics (Section 4), and narrative (Section 5) information for each occurrence of rhetorical lengthening. Based on our analysis, we found that words of all parts-of-speech categories (i.e., open-class words and closed-class clitics) can be rhetorically lengthened. In terms of their semantic or narrative effect, we found that there are two uses of RL. In Section 4, we discuss cases where rhetorical lengthening is placed on the stressed syllable of a particular word that is being enhanced for semantic effect to convey concepts such as a passage of time, intensity of a quality, or a large quantity. In Section 5, we discuss rhetorical lengthening used to enhance the narrative structure, appearing at the edge of the utterance, either at the beginning of the sentence, where it serves to provide (dis-)continuity to the previous section, or at the end of the sentence, where it serves to highlight a particularly salient word.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Overall, we find that Mrs. Jimmy Joe uses rhetorical lengthening to add meaning to certain words and this makes the performance of the story more dramatic at crucial points in the story.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: The Hul’q’umi’num’ vowel inventory consists of six short vowels /i/, /e/, /ə/, /u/, /o/, /a/, and four long vowels /i:/, /e:/, /u:/, /a:/ (Gerdts & Hukari to appear). In terms of prosodics, the acoustic effect of rhetorical lengthening is usually centered on the stressed vowel of the targeted word, and the lengthened vowel is noticeably longer than its non-lengthened counterpart.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: We measured duration, fundamental frequency f0 (which is an approximation of pitch), and intensity (loudness) in the 91 samples in order to characterize the acoustic properties of rhetorically lengthened (RL) vowels and how they compare with non-rhetorically lengthened (non-RL) vowels (cf. Boersma & Weenink 2024). The results reveal that RL vowels are approximately 1.2 seconds long and can be observed in both long and short vowels. The f0 of RL vowels is relatively higher than non-RL vowels and is mostly flat throughout its entire duration. The maximum f0 is approximately the same for both the RL and non-RL vowels in the beginning and middle of a sentence. However, the maximum f0 is lower at the end of a sentence for both non-RL and RL vowels.2

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: 3.1 Methods

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: To examine the phonetics of rhetorical lengthening, we compared vowels that are RL with vowels that are non-RL. Approximately 91 RL and 90 non-RL vowels were examined. Three measurements (commonly used in prosody) were obtained to analyze the phonetics of rhetorical lengthening: duration (in seconds), pitch (measured as the maximum f0 of the vowel), and intensity (measured as the maximum intensity of the vowel, in decibels (dB) Sound Pressure Level (SPL)), where the latter two measures were used to examine the maximum pitch and intensity displacement of vowels under the two conditions. Vowels that are underlyingly long vs. vowels that are underlyingly short in RL vs. non-RL conditions were compared.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: 2 The positions “beginning”, “middle”, and “end” are defined by Wickmann (2000).

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: We also examined the prosodic position of the word within an Intonational Phrase (IP), where IPs are identified here as prosodic domains that are separated by pauses (Nespor & Vogel 1986; Pierrehumbert & Hirschberg 1990). Three IP positions were identified: The beginning (i.e., the first stressed syllable), middle, and end (i.e., the last stressed syllable) of an IP (cf. Wickmann 2000). The software that was used to obtain acoustic measurements is Praat (Boersma & Weenenk 2024). Each recording was examined through a waveform, spectrogram, and a pitch tracker. A narrowband spectrogram was used by setting the window length in the spectrogram setting to 30ms. The pitch range was set from 100Hz (minimum) to 400Hz (maximum). The advanced pitch settings in Praat were also adjusted to capture the pitch contour of RL vowels (where the octave cost, which is a pitch parameter that tracks higher frequency candidates, was increased to capture pitch contours of RL vowels). The analysis method that was used in the pitch setting was autocorrelation.

form: Figure 8 illustrates the maximum intensity (in dB) for vowels in non-RL vs. RL conditions with respect to their position in an IP. Interestingly, the maximum intensity (in dB) in the RL condition was the lowest at the end of an IP. This is not observed in the non-RL condition, where the maximum intensity of vowels at the end of an IP was approximately the same as in the beginning or middle of an IP. This suggests that there was a strong tendency to produce a “quieter” RL vowel at the end of IPs rather than at the beginning or middle of IPs. This might be due to prosodic reasons: A quieter RL vowel can be used as a distinctive cue to mark the end of an IP (or to indicate that it “ends a sentence”); whereas in the non-RL condition, the primary cue may be declination (or falling) f0 contour at the end of IPs.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: It should be noted that most RL vowels that occurred at the end of an IP were echo repetitions (see Section 5.2 for more detail), which tend to be quieter than the main word that they repeat. This may suggest that the intensity of the RL vowel can be affected by the type of rhetorical device (such as echo repetition) used by the speaker.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: 3.3 Summary

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Rhetorical lengthening is phonetically characterized by a long duration with a high and sustained pitch contour that is quite noticeable to the human ear, and is quite apparent in the spectrogram, waveform, and pitch track evidence. Regardless of the underlying length of the vowels (i.e., short vs. long), vowels are lengthened to the same amount when rhetorically lengthened. There was also a strong tendency for Mrs. Jimmy Joe to produce RL vowels at a relatively higher pitch range than non-RL vowels across an IP. The current findings reveal that the intensity of RL vowels can differ based on their prosodic position — RL vowels at the beginning of an IP were the loudest and those at the end of an IP were the quietest.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: One impressionistic observation that is worth noting is the effect of rhetorical lengthening on vowel quality. For example, for the schwa /ə/, the vowel quality sounds lower, as in /ʌ/, when rhetorically lengthened. Another future study may require conducting an acoustic analysis on the vowel formants that compares non-RL with RL vowels. Another noteworthy observation is the variation in the length of the RL vowel for certain words. For example, the longest case of RL vowels was from the word cam ‘go up from shore’, which was 2.03 seconds, while the shortest case was from the word kʷənətəm ‘take<PAS>’, which was 0.78 seconds. The variation in duration may be due to different nuances of usage of rhetorical lengthening, a topic we hope to address in a future study.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: 4 Semantic correlates of rhetorical lengthening

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Having studied the general phonetic correlates of rhetorical lengthening, we turn in this section to a discussion of its semantic effect. As mentioned above, rhetorical lengthening can appear on a variety of word classes and in its most canonical usages, rhetorical lengthening is iconic in that it straightforwardly serves to enhance and amplify the basic meaning of the form. For example, rhetorical lengthening can convey the meaning of a long distance or passage of time on verbs, intensity of a quality on verbs and adjectives, or a large quantity or amount on quantifiers and nouns.

form: Of the 91 examples of rhetorical lengthening in Mrs. Jimmy Joe’s stories, 39 (42.8%) were on verbs and 17 (18.6%) were on auxiliaries, for a total of 56 (61.4%). We did not find any examples where neighboring auxiliaries and verbs were both rhetorically lengthened (with the exception of repetition, discussed in Section 5.1.2 below). We also could not discern why one was chosen over the other. Perhaps the best way to analyze these data is that the semantic feature of rhetorical lengthening holds for the entire event (verb complex) and the choice is free as to which word will host the phonetic feature of rhetorical lengthening — whether the auxiliary or main verb, or which of the verbs in a multi-verb clause.

form: In the corpus, we found a total of 11 examples of rhetorical lengthening on adjectives, comprising 12% of the examples with rhetorical lengthening. The adjectives lengthened were: sliqʷəl ‘calm’, kʷel̓əs ‘hot’ (50), cpxʷas ‘blonde’, ʔəy̓ ‘good’ (twice), and sʔeləxʷ ‘old’ (three times). In each instance, the function of rhetorical lengthening on the adjective is to denote intensity. Moreover, the adjectives that are expressed with rhetorical lengthening are especially important to the plot of the text, as discussed in Section 5.1 below.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Based on impressionistic observation, the RL vowels that occurred on echo repetitions sounded like they were produced with a “falsetto” and/or “whispery” voice. A research question that stems from this observation is what particular voice quality is being used by the speaker for the production of RL vowels with respect to their position in an IP. One limitation to this study is the lack of obtaining acoustic measurements that can be used to characterize differences in voice quality of RL vowels. Moreover, it is possible that the lower f0 at the end of an IP in the RL condition was due not to marking the end of an IP (which is characterized by a declination contour) but to a change in the voice quality. In general, whispery or breathy voice tends to lower f0 (Laver 1980; Gordon & Ladefoged 2001; Childers & Lee 1991). A future study may require conducting an acoustic analysis that uses these measurements to distinguish the voice qualities of RL vowels with respect to their position in an IP.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: In this study, based on 91 tokens of rhetorical lengthening from six Hul’q’umi’num’ stories told by Mrs. Jimmy Joe, we observed that rhetorical lengthening is used to direct attention to certain words or to move a listener’s attention along in the story. rhetorical lengthening is produced with a long duration and is characterized by a higher f0 (pitch) on the vowel, which is sustained throughout its total duration.12 We found that all parts of speech (both lexical and functional categories) can be rhetorically lengthened. As summarized in Table 5, verbs were most common, and we only had one example of a pro-determiner with RL.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: One interesting aspect about the placement of rhetorical lengthening is that it can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence. A more accurate way of studying it is to see if rhetorical lengthening is placed on a particular word to augment or focus it in some way. In contrast, we also see rhetorical lengthening appearing on the first element of a story or section, even if it is a small, semantically unsalient word such as a connective or auxiliary verb. In this usage, it draws the listener’s attention to the start of a new section, for example after a passage of time in the storyline. Another way to convey this would be by using a long pause between sections, but a preliminary look at this suggests that sometimes there is no pause at all between sections, and rhetorical lengthening might in fact be a better indicator of section boundaries.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Our research on rhetorical lengthening is part of a project to study the kinds of structures that one needs to master in order to be able to tell a Hul’q’umi’num’ story that sounds truly authentic and engages the audience. Rhetorical lengthening is one device that all speakers and listeners are aware of and we hope that this study aids in the appreciation of the virtuosity of the use of rhetorical lengthening by Hul’q’umi’num’ storytellers. Overall, we find that Mrs. Jimmy Joe’s use of rhetorical lengthening makes the performance of the story more dramatic at crucial points in the storyline. By studying performances by first language speakers, we hope to become more dramatic storytellers ourselves.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: One question that arises is whether or not rhetorical lengthening also shows up in conversations or other genres besides storytelling, and the preliminary answer is that we have in fact heard it used in conversations, especially for augmenting the semantics of a word (Section 3). We look forward to researching this further in our corpus of conversations.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: To our knowledge, this study is the first in-depth treatment of rhetorical lengthening in a Salish language. We have observed speakers of other Salish languages using rhetorical lengthening in a similar way, and it will be interesting to compare their acoustic and semantic properties. A final observation is that second language speakers are aware that first language speakers of Hul’q’umi’num’ also use rhetorical lengthening with similar pitch and function when they speak English. It will be interesting to compare rhetorical lengthening as used by speakers of different levels of fluency.

who: Donna Gerdts, Thomas Johnny and Ted Kye
form: Also left for future research is comparing our analysis of Hul’q’umi’num’ with rhetorical lengthening in other languages of the world. This seems to be a popular narrative device in many languages and many aspects of it might prove to be fairly universal as the voice is used iconically to convey meanings such as distance, duration, and intensity. We hope that this study contributes to a typology of rhetorical lengthening and other narrative devices.
